title: "Virtual Environment and pip"
---

::: {.callout-note}
**Goal:** Create an isolated Python workspace, activate it, and upgrade `pip` so ADK installs cleanly.
:::

## Why Use a Virtual Environment?

- Keeps ADK and its libraries separate from system Python.
- Allows experiments without risking other projects.
- Makes it easy to recreate the setup by sharing the commands.

::: {.callout-tip}
Run the commands from the folder where you want to store your ADK projects, such as `Documents/adk`.
:::

## macOS Terminal

<div class="cmd-explain">Create a virtual environment named `.venv` using Python 3.11:</div>
```bash
python3.11 -m venv .venv
```

<div class="cmd-explain">Activate the environment (notice the `(.venv)` prefix in your prompt):</div>
```bash
source .venv/bin/activate
```

<div class="cmd-explain">Upgrade `pip` inside the activated environment:</div>
```bash
python -m pip install --upgrade pip
```

## Windows PowerShell

<div class="cmd-explain">Create the `.venv` folder using the Python 3.11 interpreter:</div>
```powershell
python -m venv .venv
```

<div class="cmd-explain">Activate the environment for the current PowerShell session:</div>
```powershell
.\\.venv\\Scripts\\Activate.ps1
```

<div class="cmd-explain">Upgrade `pip` while the environment is active:</div>
```powershell
python -m pip install --upgrade pip
```

::: {.callout-check}
After activation, the prompt starts with `(.venv)` and `python --version` reports 3.11.x. If `Activate.ps1` is blocked, set the execution policy using `Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope CurrentUser RemoteSigned` and retry.
:::

Stay inside the activated environment for the remaining setup steps.
